answer.policy_title: Hip Arthroplasty - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletin
answer.effective_date: Not stated on the publicly available policy page
criteria_quotes: Aetna considers an Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved metal-on-metal, metal-on-plastic, ceramic-on-plastic, or ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty (THA) prosthesis medically necessary for adult members when the following criteria are met.

Member has advanced joint disease demonstrated by: Pain and functional disability that interferes with activities of daily living (ADLs) from injury due to osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, or post-traumatic arthritis of the hip joint; and Limited range of motion (ROM), antalgic gait, and pain in hip joint with passive ROM on physical examination; and Radiographic evidence of either of the following: Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) with stage II or III disease; or Moderate/severe osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis of the hip joint (Tonnis grade 2 or 3).

History of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/BMI) that is clearly addressed in the medical record with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) in the past year.

Members with osteoarthritis, traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or avascular necrosis should have at least 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment documented in the medical record (at least 24 weeks for persons with a relative contraindication), including all of the following, unless contraindicated: Anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics; flexibility and muscle strengthening exercises and activity modification; supervised physical therapy; assistive device use for persons with relative contraindications; and therapeutic injections into the hip for persons with relative contraindications.
If conservative therapy is not appropriate, the medical record must clearly document why such approach is not reasonable.

Total joint replacement is considered not medically necessary in persons with any of the following absolute contraindications: Active infection of the joint or active systemic bacteremia that has not been totally eradicated; active skin infection or open wound within the planned surgical site; allergy to components of the implant; corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty; paraplegia or quadriplegia; permanent or irreversible muscle weakness in the absence of pain that prevents ambulation; rapidly progressive neurological disease except in the specified displaced femoral neck fracture situation; or skeletal immaturity.
If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to hip arthroplasty.
answer.appeal_deadline: 2027-02-10, according to the denial letter: 180 days from the August 14, 2026 notice date
answer.submission_route: Submit the appeal by calling Aetna Member Services at the telephone number on the member ID card, or in writing to the address shown on the denial letter or EOB. Aetna's current Member Complaint and Appeal Form also identifies this route: mail to Aetna, P.O. Box 14463, Lexington, KY 40512, or fax to 859-425-3379. Include the member ID, reference number POC-5FADD4BBDE-47544, the requested pre-service procedure (CPT 27130), the denial date, an explanation of the appeal, and supporting clinical records and imaging. The official form is https://www.aetna.com/document-library/data/forms_library/68192.pdf
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: The publicly available Aetna CPB 0287 contains criteria for CPT 27130-related total hip arthroplasty, but its public page does not state an effective or last-revised date and the denial letter does not identify the policy number or version used. Ask Aetna Member Services, using the number on the ID card, for the exact medical policy or clinical review criteria and version applied to this prior-authorization request, including the imaging standard, the clinical-reviewer's rationale, and any plan-specific criteria. Aetna's member denial page states that members may call Member Services to request documents needed for an appeal.
answer.confidence: High that CPB 0287 is Aetna's publicly available policy containing the relevant total hip arthroplasty criteria; moderate that it is the exact version applied to this particular denial because the notice does not identify the policy number or version and the public page does not provide a revision date.
answer.notes: The policy specifically requires radiographic evidence of stage II or III avascular necrosis or moderate/severe osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis, in addition to symptoms, functional limitation, examination findings, and conservative-treatment documentation. The public policy page is subject to change, so the patient should request the version in effect for the August 14, 2026 determination.

    Procedure code (CPT): 27130

After review, this request is DENIED. Reason for determination: the imaging findings submitted do not support the medical necessity of the requested procedure.

This determination was made under the plan's applicable medical policy and clinical review criteria. You have the right to appeal this decision. Your appeal must be received within 180 days of the date of this notice (by 2027-02-10).

{"url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/200_299/0287.html", "final_url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/200_299/0287.html", "http_status": 200, "content_type": "text/html", "login_wall": false, "blocked": false, "blocked_reason": null, "error": null, "text": "Hip Arthroplasty - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins | Aetna --> Top Hip Arthroplasty Clinical Policy Bulletins Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins Print Share Number: 0287 Table Of Contents Policy Applicable CPT / HCPCS / ICD-10 Codes Background References Policy Scope of Policy This Clinical Policy Bulletin addresses hip arthroplasty. Note: Precertification may be required for select procedures and interventions. Use the CPT code search tool to see if precertification is required. Medical Necessity Aetna considers an Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved metal-on-metal, metal-on-plastic, ceramic-on-plastic, or ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty (THA) prosthesis medically necessary for adult members when the following criteria are met (see also Additional Note ): Member has advanced joint disease demonstrated by: Pain and functional disability that interferes with activities of daily living (ADLs) from injury due to osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, or post-traumatic arthritis of the hip joint; and Limited range of motion (ROM), antalgic gait, and pain in hip joint with passive ROM on physical examination: and Radiographic evidence of either of the following: Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) with stage II or III disease; or Moderate/severe osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis of the hip joint (Tonnis grade 2 or 3; see Appendix for Tonnis grading scale); and History of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/BMI) that is clearly addressed in the medical record with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) in the past year Footnote1 * . Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. If conservative therapy is not appropriate (such as for progressive flexion contracture, avascular necrosis with collapse of the femoral head, or bone on bone arthritis in the weight-bearing portion of the joint for example), the medical record must clearly document why such approach is not reasonable; or Fracture of the femoral neck by imaging; or Malunion of acetabular, femoral head or proximal femur fracture with pain interfering with ADLs; or Nonunion by imaging or failure of previous hip fracture surgery; or Malignancy of the joint involving the bones or soft tissues of the pelvis or proximal femur by imaging; Footnote1 * Note : Members with osteoarthritis, traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or avascular necrosis should have at least 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment documented in the medical record (at least 24 weeks for persons with a relative contraindication Footnote2 ** ), including all of the following, unless contraindicated: Anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics; and Flexibility and muscle strengthening exercises, and Activity modification; and Supervised physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy; ADLs diminished despite completing a plan of care). Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history; and Assistive device use (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others); and Therapeutic injections into the hip (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others); or Footnote2 ** Relative contraindications to joint replacement include the following: morbid obesity (body mass index (BMI) greater than 40), age less than 50 years). Persons with relative contraindications should exhaust all non-surgical treatment options. Total joint replacement is considered not medically necessary in persons with any of the following absolute contraindications: Active infection of the joint or active systemic bacteremia that has not been totally eradicated; or Active skin infection (exception recurrent cutaneous staph infections) or open wound within the planned surgical site of the hip; or Allergy to components of the implant (e.g., cobalt, chromium or alumina); or Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty; or Paraplegia or quadriplegia; or Permanent or irreversible muscle weakness in the absence of pain that prevents ambulation; or Rapidly progressive neurological disease except in the clinical situation of a concomitant displaced femoral neck fracture; or Skeletal immaturity; or For persons with significant conditions or co-morbidities, the risk/benefit of THA should be appropriately addressed in the medical record. Aetna considers THA experimental, investigational, or unproven for all other indications because of insufficient evidence of effectiveness. Revision or replacement of a THA or hip resurfacing arthroplasty is considered medically necessary when accompanied by pain and functional disability (interference with ADLs) when the following criteria are met (see also Additional Note ): Member has one or more of the following indications for revision or replacement: Aseptic loosening of one or more prosthetic components confirmed by imaging, or Fracture or mechanical failure of 1 or more components of the prosthesis confirmed by imaging, or Confirmed periprosthetic infection confirmed by gram stain and culture ( Note: A single stage revision is considered medically necessary for this indication, unless there has been a prior infection in the same joint, in which case a multi-stage revision may be considered medically necessary), or Displaced periprosthetic fracture confirmed by imaging, or Progressive or substantial periprosthetic bone loss confirmed by imaging, or Bearing surface wear leading to symptomatic synovitis or local bone or soft tissue reaction Footnote3 *** , or Recurrent (2 or more) dislocations confirmed by imaging not responsive to a reasonable course of conservative management or irreducible dislocation confirmed by imaging; or Clinically significant leg length discrepancy; and The member does not have any of the following contraindications to total hip revision or replacement: Loss of musculature (in particular hip abductor musculature), neuromuscular compromise or vascular deficiency in the affected limb, rendering the procedure unjustifiable; or Osteoporosis or other osseous abnormalities which would make the likelihood of a poor outcome more probable; or Poor skin coverage; or Severe instability due to anatomic causes that would make the likelihood of a poor surgical outcome more probable. Aetna considers a revision or replacement of a THA or hip resurfacing experimental, investigational, or unproven when criteria are not met. Aetna considers the following medically necessary: FDA-approved custom-made implant for Paprosky type III acetabular defects where the feature of the defect cannot be handled with standard implants, and member meets criteria for revision total hip arthroplasty listed above; Iliopsoas tenotomy (or lengthening) by any surgical approach for iliopsoas tendinopathy following total hip arthroplasty with the failure of at least 6 weeks of formal in-person physical therapy in the past year, and at least 1 therapeutic injection (steroid with or without local anesthetic) with significant but temporary benefit in the past 6 months ; Minimal incision or minimally invasive THA an acceptable alternative to conventional THA; Prophylactic use of tranexamic acid in total hip arthroplasty to decrease blood loss. Additional Note If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to hip arthroplasty. {"url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/200_299/0287.html?print=true", "final_url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/200_299/0287.html?print=true", "http_status": 200, "content_type": "text/html", "login_wall": false, "blocked": false, "blocked_reason": null, "error": null, "text": "Hip Arthroplasty - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins | Aetna --> Top Hip Arthroplasty Clinical Policy Bulletins Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins Print Share Number: 0287 Table Of Contents Policy Applicable CPT / HCPCS / ICD-10 Codes Background References Policy Scope of Policy This Clinical Policy Bulletin addresses hip arthroplasty. Note: Precertification may be required for select procedures and interventions. Use the CPT code search tool to see if precertification is required. Medical Necessity Aetna considers an Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved metal-on-metal, metal-on-plastic, ceramic-on-plastic, or ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty (THA) prosthesis medically necessary for adult members when the following criteria are met (see also Additional Note ): Member has advanced joint disease demonstrated by: Pain and functional disability that interferes with activities of daily living (ADLs) from injury due to osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, or post-traumatic arthritis of the hip joint; and Limited range of motion (ROM), antalgic gait, and pain in hip joint with passive ROM on physical examination: and Radiographic evidence of either of the following: Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) with stage II or III disease; or Moderate/severe osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis of the hip joint (Tonnis grade 2 or 3; see Appendix for Tonnis grading scale); and History of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/BMI) that is clearly addressed in the medical record with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) in the past year Footnote1 * . Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. If conservative therapy is not appropriate (such as for progressive flexion contracture, avascular necrosis with collapse of the femoral head, or bone on bone arthritis in the weight-bearing portion of the joint for example), the medical record must clearly document why such approach is not reasonable; or Fracture of the femoral neck by imaging; or Malunion of acetabular, femoral head or proximal femur fracture with pain interfering with ADLs; or Nonunion by imaging or failure of previous hip fracture surgery; or Malignancy of the joint involving the bones or soft tissues of the pelvis or proximal femur by imaging; Footnote1 * Note : Members with osteoarthritis, traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or avascular necrosis should have at least 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment documented in the medical record (at least 24 weeks for persons with a relative contraindication Footnote2 ** ), including all of the following, unless contraindicated: Anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics; and Flexibility and muscle strengthening exercises, and Activity modification; and Supervised physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy; ADLs diminished despite completing a plan of care). Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history; and Assistive device use (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others); and Therapeutic injections into the hip (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others); or Footnote2 ** Relative contraindications to joint replacement include the following: morbid obesity (body mass index (BMI) greater than 40), age less than 50 years). Persons with relative contraindications should exhaust all non-surgical treatment options. Total joint replacement is considered not medically necessary in persons with any of the following absolute contraindications: Active infection of the joint or active systemic bacteremia that has not been totally eradicated; or Active skin infection (exception recurrent cutaneous staph infections) or open wound within the planned surgical site of the hip; or Allergy to components of the implant (e.g., cobalt, chromium or alumina); or Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty; or Paraplegia or quadriplegia; or Permanent or irreversible muscle weakness in the absence of pain that prevents ambulation; or Rapidly progressive neurological disease except in the clinical situation of a concomitant displaced femoral neck fracture; or Skeletal immaturity; or For persons with significant conditions or co-morbidities, the risk/benefit of THA should be appropriately addressed in the medical record. Aetna considers THA experimental, investigational, or unproven for all other indications because of insufficient evidence of effectiveness. Revision or replacement of a THA or hip resurfacing arthroplasty is considered medically necessary when accompanied by pain and functional disability (interference with ADLs) when the following criteria are met (see also Additional Note ): Member has one or more of the following indications for revision or replacement: Aseptic loosening of one or more prosthetic components confirmed by imaging, or Fracture or mechanical failure of 1 or more components of the prosthesis confirmed by imaging, or Confirmed periprosthetic infection confirmed by gram stain and culture ( Note: A single stage revision is considered medically necessary for this indication, unless there has been a prior infection in the same joint, in which case a multi-stage revision may be considered medically necessary), or Displaced periprosthetic fracture confirmed by imaging, or Progressive or substantial periprosthetic bone loss confirmed by imaging, or Bearing surface wear leading to symptomatic synovitis or local bone or soft tissue reaction Footnote3 *** , or Recurrent (2 or more) dislocations confirmed by imaging not responsive to a reasonable course of conservative management or irreducible dislocation confirmed by imaging; or Clinically significant leg length discrepancy; and The member does not have any of the following contraindications to total hip revision or replacement: Loss of musculature (in particular hip abductor musculature), neuromuscular compromise or vascular deficiency in the affected limb, rendering the procedure unjustifiable; or Osteoporosis or other osseous abnormalities which would make the likelihood of a poor outcome more probable; or Poor skin coverage; or Severe instability due to anatomic causes that would make the likelihood of a poor surgical outcome more probable. Aetna considers a revision or replacement of a THA or hip resurfacing experimental, investigational, or unproven when criteria are not met. Aetna considers the following medically necessary: FDA-approved custom-made implant for Paprosky type III acetabular defects where the feature of the defect cannot be handled with standard implants, and member meets criteria for revision total hip arthroplasty listed above; Iliopsoas tenotomy (or lengthening) by any surgical approach for iliopsoas tendinopathy following total hip arthroplasty with the failure of at least 6 weeks of formal in-person physical therapy in the past year, and at least 1 therapeutic injection (steroid with or without local anesthetic) with significant but temporary benefit in the past 6 months ; Minimal incision or minimally invasive THA an acceptable alternative to conventional THA; Prophylactic use of tranexamic acid in total hip arthroplasty to decrease blood loss. Additional Note If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to hip arthroplasty. Experimental, Investigational, or Unproven The following are considered experimental, investigational, or unproven because the effectiveness of the approach has not been established: Augmented or virtual reality (AR/VR) assistance for hip arthroplasty Computer-assisted surgical navigation (e.g., MAKOplasty/MAKO Tactile Guidance System) for total hip replacement (THR) because there is a lack of reliable evidence that it improves clinical outcomes of THA Note: Robotic assistance is considered integral to the procedure and not separately reimbursed Custom joint implants and/or instrumentation Measurement of synovial C-reactive protein, and the alpha-defensin test (Synovasure) as a marker for peri-prosthetic infection in THA Obturator nerve blocks for management of post-operative pain following THA Pre-operative advanced imaging that is required for any experimental, investigational, or unproven procedure (e.g., where required for computer-assisted surgical navigation, robotic-assisted surgical navigation, or for customized patient implants and/or instrumentation) The use of a portable accelerometer-based navigation system because its clinical value has not been established. See also CPB 0710 - Actigraphy and Accelerometry . Footnote3 *** Aetna considers removal and revision surgery due to post-THR metallosis alone, without evidence of loosening or malposition, experimental, investigational, or unproven because there is insufficient clinical evidence in the published peer-reviewed medical literature. Related CMS Coverage Guidance This Clinical Policy Bulletin (CPB) supplements but does not replace, modify, or supersede existing Medicare Regulations or applicable National Coverage Determinations (NCDs) or Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs). The supplemental medical necessity criteria in this CPB further define those indications for services that are proven safe and effective where those indications are not fully established in applicable NCDs and LCDs. These supplemental medical necessity criteria are based upon evidence-based guidelines and clinical studies in the peer-reviewed published medical literature. The background section of this CPB includes an explanation of the rationale that supports adoption of the medical necessity criteria and a summary of evidence that was considered during the development of the CPB; the reference section includes a list of the sources of such evidence. While there is a possible risk of reduced or delayed care with any coverage criteria, Aetna believes that the benefits of these criteria – ensuring patients receive services that are appropriate, safe, and effective – substantially outweigh any clinical harms. This CPB is being used to supplement Medicare LCDs on hip arthroplasty (Total Joint (Hip/Knee) – LCD L33456, LCD L33618, LCD L36007, LCD L36039; Total Hip – LCD L34163, LCD L36573). This CPB is used to define appropriate conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management), as some patients may respond to conservative therapy (see, e.g., Conley, et al., 2023; Fernandes, et al., 2013; Fransen, et al., 2014; Goh, et al., 2019; Sampath, et al., 2016; Sasaki, et al., 2022), avoiding the need for surgery and its inherent risks (see, e.g., Agodi, et al., 2017; Dale, et al., 2011; Davidson, et al., 2008; DeHart, et al., 1999; Desai, et al., 2013; Gundtoft, et al., 2015; Januel, et al., 2002; Lieberman, et al., 2017; Lindeque, et al., 2014; Morrey, et al., 1997; Pinson, et al., 2014; Saleh, et al., 2002; Schmalzried, et al., 1997; Sharma, et al., 2003). We believe the clinical benefits of avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful care outweighs any potential risks in delayed or reduced access to care.
